newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania's Hungarians blast charges of disloyalty.
newsitem.headline: Romania's Hungarians blast charges of disloyalty.

text.p: Romania's ethnic Hungarians on Wednesday branded as "grotesque and stupid" calls by the head of the defeated leftist party to keep them out of the new government on grounds they would leak information to Budapest.

The fury unleashed at comments by Adrian Nastase, Executive President of the Party of Social Democracy (PDSR), threatened to rekindle ethnic tensions between Romanians and the country's 1.6 million ethnic Hungarians.

Hungarians voted solidly for President-elect Emil Constantinescu, who ousted ex-Communist Ion iliescu in this month's elections and is to be sworn in on Friday. Their representatives will get at least one cabinet post in discussions between three coalition partners.
Local media quoted Nastase as telling reporters on Tuesday that it was dangerous to include the Hungarian Democratic Union (UDMR) in the new government.
"The UDMR's participation in the government will mean that everything discussed at cabinet meetings will be known in Budapest," Nastase was quoted as saying.
"This is grotesque and stupid," UDMR senator Karoly Szabo told Reuters during a session of parliament devoted to electing chairmen for both houses of parliament.
"This is an attempt to split the coalition partners and a serious violation of the constitution. What easier and cheaper accusation than to say citizens of this country are spying?"
In Budapest, a Hungarian Foreign Ministry spokesman told Reuters he was surprised and puzzled at comments made by Nastase, Romania's Foreign Minister in the early 1990s.
"Such comments are completely unfounded and we are surprised to hear them from such an important political personality as Mr Nastase," Gabor Szentivanyi said.
Romanians and Hungarians have had troubled relations for centuries in central Europe.

An historic treaty signed by the two neighbours in September was intended to allay fears by Romanian nationalists that Hungary would attempt to recover parts of Transylvania, which it once ruled as part of the Austro-Hungarian empire.
Iliescu attacked the UDMR during the election campaign, saying it was plotting Yugoslav-style secession in a last-ditch attempt to strike at the core of Romanian emotions.
Like Nastase, Iliescu suggested then that putting ethnic Hungarians into office would create a "worrying situation".

Prime Minister-designate Victor Ciorbea will seek approval for his cabinet next week, with most jobs going to Constantinescu's Democratic Covention (CDR) and the junior coalition partner, the Social Democrats (USD). The UDMR is expected to get the tourism ministry and a secondary post.

At Wednesday's session, the Senate elected as its chairman USD leader Petre Roman, Iliescu's first post-Communist prime minister who was removed from office after leftist miners sacked central Bucharest in 1991.

Roman, now the number two state official, defeated the PDSR candidate, outgoing Foreign Minister Teodor Melescanu. The lower house, the Chamber of Deputies, elected Ion Diaconescu, head of the National Peasant Party, the CDR's main party.
